en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Introduction to the Chapter on Puzzling Questions;
The Section on the Qualities of a Lay Follower.
1. The Eight Places to be Avoided by a Wise Man:
One who indulges in frivolous talk, a sophist, one with excessive intellect, and one who is overly clever;
Milinda approached Nāgasena for the sake of discerning his wisdom;
he dwelt in the shade of that tree.
By asking questions again and again,
he too, having attained analytical wisdom,
became a master of the Three Piṭakas.
While reflecting upon the ninefold [scripture] in solitude during the latter part of the night,
he beheld the Meṇḍaka questions.
Difficult to unravel and difficult to restrain:
“There is that which was spoken by way of a method;
there is that which was spoken with intentional reference.”
There is that which is illuminated by its own intrinsic nature within the teaching of the Dhamma King; yet,
without understanding their meaning, [one remains ignorant].
Regarding the *Meṇḍaka* spoken by the Victor:
in a future time,
there will be a dispute concerning it.
Now, having appeased Kathika,
I shall have Menḍaka executed along the path he has indicated.
“They shall explain it in the future.
Then King Milinda, when the night had turned to dawn and the sun had risen, bathed his head, raised his joined palms in reverence,
and having recollected the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, future, and present, undertook eight rules of conduct.
“From now on, for seven days, I shall practice asceticism after undertaking eight precepts;
having practiced asceticism and satisfied my teacher, I will ask him about the Meṇḍaka questions.
Then King Milinda removed his pair of natural silk garments, took off his ornaments, and put on the saffron robe.
Having fastened a shaven-head cap upon his head and attained the state of a sage, he undertook eight qualities:
"For these seven days, I must not exercise the functions of kingship; I must not give rise to a mind associated with lust;
I must not give rise to a mind associated with hatred; I must not give rise to a mind associated with delusion; [I must not employ] slaves, laborers, or servants..."
"One should live with a humble disposition even among people; one’s bodily and verbal actions should be guarded;
the six sense bases should be guarded without exception; and the mind should be directed toward the cultivation of loving-kindness.
Having undertaken these eight qualities and having established the mind in those very eight qualities, without going outside—
Having spent seven days, on the eighth day at the break of dawn, he first took his morning meal; then, with downcast eyes, speaking in moderation,
with a well-composed deportment, an undistracted mind, joyful, elated, and serene,
he approached the Elder Nāgasena, bowed his head at the Elder’s feet, and standing to one side, said this:

“Venerable Nāgasena, there is a certain matter I wish to discuss with you; no third person should be desired to be present there. It should be in a secluded place in the forest, empty and remote, suitable for a recluse and endowed with the eight factors.

There that question shall be asked; there I must not be made to feel it is a secret or a mystery, for I am worthy to hear a secret when approached for consultation. That matter should also be examined by means of a simile.”
"Just as, Venerable Nāgasena, the great earth is worthy of receiving a burden when a burden has arrived;
even so, Venerable Nāgasena, am I worthy to hear the secret doctrine now that the time for its recitation has arrived.
Having entered the secluded forest together with his teacher, he said this:

“Venerable Nāgasena, here, when a man wishes to deliberate on a matter, there are eight places that should be avoided; a wise man does not deliberate on a matter in those places, for even if a matter is deliberated upon there, it fails and does not succeed.
What are the eight places?
A place that is uneven should be avoided; a place that is dangerous should be avoided; a place with a strong wind should be avoided.”
“A secluded place is to be avoided; a shrine is to be avoided; a path is to be avoided;
a battlefield is to be avoided; a watering place is to be avoided.
These eight places are to be avoided.”
The Elder asked:
"What is the fault in an uneven place, a dangerous place, a windy place, a concealed place, a shrine of a deity, a path, a battlefield, or a river crossing?
"Venerable Nāgasena, in an uneven place, a matter that has been deliberated upon is scattered, dispersed, leaked away, and does not come to fruition."
In a place of danger, the mind becomes agitated; being agitated, one does not correctly perceive the meaning.
In a strong wind, a sound becomes indistinct; in a concealed place, people stand eavesdropping. In a divine sanctuary, a matter deliberated upon turns out significant;
on a public road, a matter deliberated upon becomes trivial. In battle, it becomes wavering; at a water-ford, it becomes exposed.
It is said here:
"Uneven, dangerous, with excessive wind,
concealed, and inhabited by deities."
“The road, a battle, and a ford—
these eight one should avoid.
These are the eight places to be avoided when deliberating.
